MAYOR WHEELER WEDS. Springfield's Chief Officer Married to Former Teacher. REPUBLIC SPECIAL. Springfield, Ill., Aug. 22—Mayor Loren E. Wheeler, and Miss Maud Hoffman, both of this city, were married at 2 o'clock this afternoon at the home of the bride's parents, Mr. and Mrs. Philip Hoffman. The ceremony was performed by the Reverend E. B. Rogers, pastor of the Central Baptist Church. The wedding was a general surprise, although it had been whispered about by some of their intimate friends that Mayor Wheeler and Miss Hoffman were to wed. Few knew the date, and every precaution was taken to keep it a secret. The Mayor was at his office in the City Hall this morning, and when the subject of his marriage was mentioned to him it failed to elicit any information. Mayor Wheeler is now serving his second term of office. After the ceremony he and his bride left for a trip to Denver and other places of interest. Mrs. Wheeler is a graduate of the Springfield High School and has been a teacher in one of the public schools. NEGRO KILLED WHITE MAN. Mob, Headed by the Victim's Brother, Looking for the Slayer.
REPUBLIC SPECIAL.

Judsonia, Ark., Aug. 22—Charlie Green, a negro, shot and killed Will Eaton, a white man, who lives near Poplar Bluff. The shooting occurred at this place this evening. Several shots were fired by each man, but the negro fired first and last, bringing Eaton down at the second shot.

When Will Eaton fell, his brother, Tom Eaton, took the revolver from his brother's hand and pursued the negro, who escaped to a corn field near by.

The Constable and a large number of citizens are scouring the country for the negro.

MOB AFTER A NEGRO.

St. Joseph Policeman Protected His Prisoner During a Mile Run.

REPUBLIC SPECIAL.

St. Joseph, Mo., Aug. 22—A mob of infuriated white men chased Police Officer Kieffer and Bud Wilson, a negro prisoner, aged 18 years, for a distance of a mile through the Chicago Great Western Railroad yards.

But for the officer's efforts to protect his prisoner, Wilson would have been lynched. The negro is in a cell at the police station awaiting the outcome of injuries inflicted upon M. F. Lyon, a brakeman, who was stabbed by him in the abdomen. Wilson was stealing a ride.

Shot by a Neyro
Cheneyville, La., August 10.—In a shooting here this afternoon Benny Wall, aged 21, was shot and killed by Joseph Hamilton, a negro. The latter was severely wounded, having his leg broken by one of Wall's bullets. Hamilton was arrested. Nothing is known about the cause of the trouble between the two men.

RACE DIFFICULTY LEADS TO BLOODSHED.
YOUNG WHITE MAN KILLED BY LOUISIANA NEGRO-LYNCHING PREVENTED.
YOUNG WHITE MAN KILLED BY LOUISIANA
NEGRO—LYNCHING PREVENTED.

New-Orleans, Aug. 11 (Special).—The incompatibility of the white and black races led to the killing of a young white man to-day and the serious wounding of a negro. The affair occurred at Cheneyville, La. Benjamin Wall and Samuel Blum, young white men, were walking on a plankwalk from Cheneyville to Theoda. The walk consists of two narrow boards side by side. Half way between the two settlements Wall and Blum met a negro named Joseph Milton, who was out walking with his sweetheart. Blum and Wall stepped to the left, walking single file, but the negroes refused to unlock arms, and Milton brushed heavily against Wall. The white man resented the conduct with a blow. Milton walked a few steps and drew a revolver. Wall followed suit, and a pistol duel followed, each firing four shots. Wall's abdomen was penetrated, and he died in a few minutes. Milton's leg was broken and he crawled away into a cornfield. A crowd of enraged whites quickly collected, and it was with great difficulty that a lynching was averted and the negro carried to jail at Alexandria. Wall was a prominent young man.
cheneyville-cheneyville-1900-08-13.A3:
TO REGULATE NEGROES' CONDUCT. Whites of a Louisiana Parish Meet and Lay Down Rules for Various Situations.
NEW ORLEANS, La., Aug. 13.—Because of the killing of a white man, Bennie Wall, by a negro, Joe Milton, the white people of Cheney Rapids Parish have met in a public meeting and decided upon a number of rules relative to the future conduct and discipline of the negroes in that region. There was a disposition shown at first to attempt to lynch Milton, and squads of armed white men from Bunkle, Alexandria, Haasville, Iamourie and other places rode into Cheneyville and tendered their assistance. The Sheriff of the parish, however, stood firm in his determination to allow no lynching; and the regulators who rode into town were told that their services were not needed.

It was then decided to hold a conference of white residents of Cheneyville to decide upon measures to preserve peace and order. C. Cannon was called to the chair, R. H. Jackson chosen secretary. A committee of five was appointed to prepare resolutions. All negro men, idle or out of work, were ordered to leave Cheneyville. All barrooms or places where the negroes gamble by day or night, were ordered closed. All negroes found discharging firearms were to be dealt with properly and their weapons taken from them. Other resolutions are as follows:

"Whereas it is a habit of numerous negroes to congregate and sit on the depot, preventing the passage of ladies and children in entering and leaving the depot and cars, be it "Resolved that said custom be immediately abolished; that as there exists an indisposition among a saucy and impudent set of young negro men and women to yield the sidewalks and road to ladies and children, any one caught falling to do so, on being reported to the committee, shall be severely dealt with."

A committee of twenty-two was appointed to see that these resolutions be carried out, and it proceeded at once to close a number of establishments at which the negroes congregate, and to warn idle negroes to leave town. Quite an emigration set in at once. Cheneyville is the place that figures conspicuously in "Uncle Tom's Cabin."

Whipped for Getting in the Way of White Passengers. NEW ORLEANS Aug. 15-The commit-
NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 15.—The committee appointed by the recent white mass meeting in Cheneyville, La., to regulate the negroes of that neighborhood, went to work yesterday. The resolutions adopted ordered the negroes to give way on the sidewalk to white people and also prohibited them from gathering at the railroad depot.

A young negro, Walter Brown, jumped on a railroad train today, and got in the way of some white passengers. It was decided by the committee to discipline him. He was, therefore, marched to the business centre of the town, straightened out, and given fifty lashes with a cowhide whip, in the presence of a large audience of whites and negroes.

CITY BREVITIES.
It has been announced that the Houston public schools will open for the next session on September 17.

Mrs. Mary J. Briscoe will be 81 years old today. She will be glad to receive her friends between 5 and 7 p.m.

Houston Council No. 59, U. C. T., will hold an important meeting at Knights of Pythias hall Saturday evening at 8 o'clock.

There are undelivered telegrams at the Western Union Telegraph company's office for W. T. Johnson and W. D. Childs.

Justice Hill performed the marriage ceremony for Sol Gordon and Miss Lillie Cliffe Wednesday at his home. Both the contracting parties live in Houston.

The police force was weaker last night than it has been for some time, having been short eight officers. The mounted men had to be utilized on beats.

William Reddick was bound over in Justice Malsch's court yesterday. The charge against him is aggravated assault, and the amount of his bond was fixed at $300.

Yesterday at the regular shoot of the Bering Gun club, at their grounds, Mr. C. L. Bering won the medal from Mr. L. D. Harvey, who has held it during the past week.

The members of the Houston Light Guard contemplate giving an individual competitive drill and social entertainment on August 29, at their armory and rooms, on Main street and Capitol avenue.

Deputy Sheriff Wilson left for Terrell yesterday afternoon, having in custody four negroes who had been declared insane. The negroes will be confined in the North Texas Hospital for the Insane.

There will be a number of informal races among small boats at Morgans Point Sunday. The Houston Aquatic club will participate in the events, which will be conducted purely for sport.

At the meeting of sportsmen held Wednesday evening it was decided not to hold a State shoot, but to have a local shoot in connection with the Labor Day celebration, September 3, at Magnolia park.

On account of the absence of the pastor, Rev. S. M. Tenney, there will be no services at the Second Presbyterian church Sunday morning. Rev. W. H. Leavell will hold the night services at 8:30. A full attendance of the church members is desired.

The Post's information regarding the case came direct, but was given erroneously.

The remains of the little girl were buried at Willis at 5 o'clock yesterday evening. The family will be absent from the city for two weeks.

thomas-j-amos-cheneyville-1900-08-29.A2:
"SEE HOW A MAN CAN DIE." A Negro Murderer's Challenge to a Mob That Was About to Hang Him.
CHENEYVILLE, La., Aug. 29.—Alanson G. Jackson, a storekeeper on the Bennettville plantation, near Cheneyville, was assassinated by Thomas J. Amos, a negro, last night. The murderer was captured by a mob shortly before daylight this morning and taken to the scene of his crime and lynched. Two weeks ago Jackson had a difficulty with Amos, and the negro, it is said, had threatened the merchant several times since the trouble. Last night Jackson attended a ball at Cheneyville and on his return home was fired upon from ambush and instantly killed. A mob was soon organized, and suspicion pointing to Amos on account of his threats, started for the black man's home. As soon as the squad was seen approaching the house the negro caught up his gun and attempted to fire into them. This he was prevented from doing by his aged father, who wrenched the gun from his grasp and who turned him over to the crowd. The prisoner was then taken back to the store, where he made a confession.

After the confession the murderer was taken to a convenient tree, and while preparations were being made for the hanging bee he exclaimed:

"Tie your rope over a limb and I'll slip my head in the noose and climb the tree and jump off, and show you how a man can die."

He also invited the crowd to shoot into his body, and "see how a man can die."

In less than an hour the incident was closed, the Coroner was notified and the body was left swinging on the tree.
thomas-j-amos-cheneyville-1900-08-29.A3:
LYNCHING FOLLOWED MURDER.
Mob Wreaked Its Vengeance for a Bloody Assassination.
New Orleans, Aug. 29.—A special to the Picayune from Cheneyville, La., says:

A most dastardly assassination was perpetrated at Bennetville on Bayou Bouof, five miles below this place, last night, at Bennet's store.

Alanson G. Jackson, who had charge of the store, attended a dance at Cheneyville. Later he returned to the store, and just before getting to the steps, which led to a gallery in the rear part of the building, he was fired upon with a double-barrelled gun at a distance of 30 feet, both barrels loaded with buckshot and both taking effect. One charge went through from the side of the head, the other striking him in the forehead and arms.

The assassin then threw out the shells and put in fresh ones, loaded with bird-shot, after which he approached his victim, who was lying dead, and putting the gun in close proximity to the body of Jackson, fired both barrels into the lower limbs. The assassin was Thomas J. Amos, colored.

After killing Jackson the murderer went to the home of his father, who lived a mile from the store and remained there until arrested. The prisoner was taken back to the store and questioned by those present, when he made a full confession. After the confession he was taken to a convenient tree, and, while preparations were being made for a hanging bee, Amos said:

"Tie your rope over a limb and I'll slip my head in the noose, climb the tree, jump off, and show you how a man can die." He also invited the crowd to shoot into his body.

In less than an hour the incident was closed, the coroner was notified and the body of Thomas Amos was left swinging in the early morning breeze as a warning to law-breakers, and those who are evilly disposed.
thomas-j-amos-cheneyville-1900-08-29.A5:
R1DDLED HIM WITH BULLETS.
A Mob Refuses a Negro's Offer to Commit Suicide.
NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 29.—Tom Amos, a negro, was lynched at Cheneyville, La., tonight for the murder of a white man named Lawson Jackson. The body of Jackson was found at an early hour this morning just in front of his house, where he had been assassinated by some one with a shotgun. Amos was suspected and arrested by a mob of white men. He confessed his guilt, but could give no reason for the murder.

He offered to commit suicide, that is to lynch himself by climbing up a tree, tearing a rope around his neck and to a limb, and then springing from the tree.

The mob, however, would not consent to this and strung him up and riddled the body with bullets.

tom-wiggins-nashville-1900-08-24.A1:
NINETEEN SHOT STRUCK.
Attempted Assassination in Nashville. Narrow Escape from Death.
Nashville, N. C., August 27.—An attempted assassination has stirred up the Mt. Pleasant section of Nash county. Friday night Mr. Manoah M. Bissett, a prominent farmer of that section, was disturbed by a noise at his barn. He investigated, but found nothing. As he turned from the barn a shot gun was fired and Mr. Bassett was struck by nineteen small shot, twelve in the head and seven in the shoulder. The wounds though severe, are not expected to be fatal.

Mr. Bissett has the reputation of being a peaceable man and it was hard to find the cause for the deed. Suspicion fell upon a negro man, Tone Wiggins, who worked in that section. He was arrested and his trial took place this morning at Mr. Bissett's house, he being too badly wounded to leave. There are threats of lynching the negro.

A State Conference to be Held in Raleigh Soon.

ATTEMPT TO ASSASSINATE.

Delegates to Consider the Industrial and Educational Interests of the Colored Raco-Gifts to St. Lukes Home—A Peaceable Farmer Shot in the Dark—Reports Show a Discouraging Outlook for the Farmers—Rain Came Too Late to Greatly Benefit Them.

Raleigh, N. C., Aug. 29.—Rev. C. H. King, of this city, president of the Negro State Conference, has called this conference to meet in this city, September 26 and 27, 1900. This conference is not a new thing, but has been in existence several years. The call will state particularly that the objects to be considered will be the industrial and educational advancement of the race and to take such steps as in the wisdom of the conference will be to their material advancement along these lines. There is a great unrest among our people at this time, said Rev. King, and this conference will allay it to a great extent.

We expect a large and representative delegation, as all eyes will be turned upon us to see what we are going to do.

The call is now in press and will be circulated all over the State.

THE CROP BULLETIN.

The Crop Bulletin for the week ending Monday, August 27th, says:

The reports of crop correspondents for the week ending, Monday, August 27th, 1900, are not encouraging. While local rains have been frequent in many eastern counties, as well as on the east slope of the Blue Ridge, from the 20th to 24th, the rainfall was pretty irregularly distributed and generally insufficient, and, though refreshing to some late crops, the effects have not lasted long, and the soil now appears to be as dry as ever. Crop conditions are more diversified than ever and more difficult to summarize. Where rains partially broke the drought late corn and cotton have been benefitted, also field peas and potatoes; and in the west sowing turnips and turning land for wheat was possible early in the week. The temperature has continued unusually high, averaging again narly 70 degrees daily above normal, and the complete absence of rain over large areas makes it impossible to consider the drought broken, or to report any material improvement in crop prospects for the State at large. On the contrary, where rains have occurred they generally came too late (except possibly over extreme eastern counties) to increase the probable yield of staple crops, which have continued to suffer fearfully in sections where no rain has fallen. Forest fires in northeastern counties have been very destructive to timber.

The great damage caused by the heat and drought to cotton has now become fully apparent; many fields present the appearance which they usually have at the end of September. Rust is reported in many counties, bolls are opening very rapidly everywhere, but the bolls are imperfect, generally being from one-half to three-fourths of full size; picking is in progress; still, late cotton in many counties was improved by rain, and late blooms are reported by correspondent at Moncure (Chatham) and Washburn (Rutherford county).

Young corn is promising only where rains have been most frequent this week; the yield of corn will unquestionably be very short; pulling fodder is still under way.

william-fiqua-chicago-1900-08-16.A2:
A NASHVILLE NEGRO
Shatches Pocket-book In Chicago and Comes Near Being Lynched.

Chicago Aug. 16.—William Fikua, a colored man from Nashville, Tenn., came dangerously near being lynched in the street to-night. He snatched a pocketbook from a woman and led the police a long chase through the alleys and downtown streets. During his flight he fired three times at the police and the crowd which followed the officers in the pursuit. He was finally caught in front of the Great Northern Hotel, where he crawled under a horse which was standing by the hotel entrance.

While the officers were taking their prisoner to the police station they were followed by a crowd fully 500 strong which shouted: "Hang him," "Lynch him," "Take him away." The officers halted at Madison and Clark streets to wait for the patrol wagon, and the crowd made a desperate effort to take Fikua from them. Ropes were procured, and if the colored man had been taken from the police he certainly would have been hanged. The police used their clubs vigorously and managed to get the prisoner to the patrol wagon, which made a successful dash through the crowd.
william-fiqua-chicago-1900-08-16.A5:
TRIED TO LYNCH NEGRO.
Chicago Mob Angered by a Colored Pickpocket.
Chicago Aug. 17. Thousands of thes
Chicago, Aug. 17.—Thousands of theater-goers and pedestrians who had come down town sight-seeing last night heard revolver shots and cries of "Hang him!" "Lynch him!" Looking about to see the cause of the commotion many were brushed aside and some trampled upon in the mad rush of a mob increasing with every step which chased William Flqua, a colored man, thru the down town streets. Flqua had snatched a pocket book from a woman at Wabash avenue and Madison street, and when Patrolman Stine of the central detail station attemted to intercept him Flqua opened fire upon him with a revolver. The shots were returned by Stine.

The sight of the crowd which gathered seemed to infuriate the negro, and he shot right and left as he fled. A Pinkerton watchman near Dearborn street and Calhoun place was shot thru the cap by a bullet from the man's revolver and he joined in the fusillade. People rushed to the scene of the shooting from all directions. Guests of the Great Northern poured out into the street. One of the crowd carried a rope.

"Hang him! Lynch him!" again shrieked the pursuers. At Adams and Dearborn streets Flqua dived under a cab horse and bade defiance to the mob. Police Brennan advanced on the man and when within ten feet was greeted by a shot from the 38-caliber revolver. Before the negro could fire a second time he was seized by Policemen Brennan, Sullivan and Dennehy.

Surrounding the prisoner closely, the policemen started to walk to the central station. The infuriated mob vainly attempted to take the prisoner away. A rope was quickly found, and the crowd again took up the cry of "Lynch him!" At Adams street a man with a loaded cane struck the negro a blow across the head, which felled him to the ground. The police closed in and the mob was forced back.

Pursued by the mob, which by this time choked the street, the policemen finally succeeded in landing the colored man at the patrol box at Madleon and Clark streets. Further advance was impossible until the patrol wagon arrived, when he was taken to the central station.

When questioned by the police the colored man claimed to have arrived two days ago from Nashville, Tenn. He was a ragged, half-starved looking negro, apparently about 30 years old, and black as a coal.

william-fiqua-chicago-1900-08-16.A19:
NARROWLY ESCAPES LYNCHING.
A Colored Thief Causes Excitement in the Streets of Chicago.
CHICAGO, Aug. 17. — Chicago came near witnessing a repetition of the New Orleans and New York anti-negro riots late last night. William Fiqua, a negro desperado, missed lynching by a hair's breadth, after being chased for blocks by an infuriated crowd of 2,000 men clamoring for his blood. He was saved only by the strenuous efforts of a large detail of police within two blocks of the City Hall.

Fiqua ran amuck from the moment he snatched a pocketbook from a woman at Madison Street and Wabash Avenue. Her scream of terror brought half a dozen men tumbling out of a cable train, and the pickpocket dashed west on Madison Street, drawing a revolver as he ran. Policeman Stine tried to stop him, but the man fired full at him, making off up an alleyway before the policeman could seize him.

Stine gave chase, firing twice at the robber, but failing to hit him. The man ran west on Washington Street to State, north on State to Holden Place, and then turned west toward Dearborn Street.

Stine followed his man, the attendant crowd growing larger every moment. The reports of revolvers brought men hurrying out of saloons, restaurants, and hotels, and as Fiqua turned south on Dearbon Street there was a crowd of 100 barring his way at Randolph Street. He charged between the throngs on the sidewalk, flourishing his revolver, and no one dared to stop him. Escape east on Washington Street was impossible, because of crowds swarming in from Clark and State Streets. Another and larger throng barred his path at Madison Street. Sending a shot toward the crowd, the thief dashed aside into Calhoun Place, doubling west toward Clark Street.

Policeman Dennehy and a Pinkerton watchman headed him for a moment in a narrow passage. Twice Fiqua fired at them, rushing by through the smoke, reloading his revolver from a supply of cartridges in his coat. John E. Mahar, a cabman, seized him, but the negro smashed his revolver butt in Mahar's face, and twisted away. After firing repeatedly at his pursuers but failing to hit anyone, the negro was finally overtaken after many twists and turns in front of the new post-office building on Michigan Avenue, where, utterly exhausted, he flung himself under a cab horse. At once he was seized by four officers and surrounded by a howling mob.

"Hang him!" "Kill the black devil!" the crowd shrieked, and the police tried to make way for the captive up Dearborn Street. Fists were battered against the negro's head and face. A man with a rope cut from an awning threw a noose over the robber's head. At Madison Street a crowd, which had been swelled to three thousand men and boys, tried to drag Figua away from his protectors. A man with a loaded cane brought it down on the negro's skull, and he slipped half way to the pavement, bleeding from a wound on his head.

Working toward the central station, the officers and their quarry ran up against an immovable barrier of excited men at Madison and Clark Streets. Despairing of breaking through the mob, which stretched a block in each direction, a riot call was sent in and Figua made the last block of his journey in a patrol wagon. He was bruised and beaten about the head and shoulders, but his injuries are not serious.

Figua declared that he had recently come from Nashville, but the police believe that he is the footpad who shot Fireman Thomas J. Honore a few days ago.
william-fiqua-chicago-1900-08-16.A21:
MONDAY, AUG. 20, 1900.
RACE HATRED IN NORTHERN STATES.
TRED IN
STATES.

There is something exceedingly sinister in the reports of riot and bloodshed between white men and black men in different parts of the country. In the city of New Orleans and in the city of New York extensive riots have occurred, the cause of which is simply racial hatred which takes advantage of a lapse from virtue on the part of an individual to threaten the whole race with death and destruction.

The origin of the riots is precisely the same in each city. A negro commits a crime against property and resists arrest. In the course of his resistance he kills a police officer. At once the white population of the neighborhood howls for vengeance, not merely upon the original offender, but upon all the negroes in the neighborhood. Mobs of white persons attack negroes wherever they find them, and the negroes, whenever possible, meet force with force. Large detachments of police charge the riotous crowds, and the negroes are captured, clubbed into submission and thrown into the police station, while the white rioters, with rare exceptions, go free.

The circumstances may be briefly described in this way:

A dozen white persons see two negro students on a street car. The car is stopped and the negroes are dragged from it and ferociously assaulted. A rope is produced, the crowd of white persons grows larger and the negroes are being hauled to a neighboring lamp post to be lynched—no not lynched, for that means a rude semblance of justice—but to be murdered, when some bystander turns in a call for the police. The police, apparently acting upon the supposition that the two negroes are assaulting the crowd of whites, seize upon the colored men, club them into insensibility and carry them off to jail or hospital. And this—because a tough negro a day or so before had killed a policeman. If the slayer of the policeman had been white the crime would have excited but little comment and certainly not have caused riots.

But racial antipathy was formed into dangerous frenzy by the crime of the black against the white man, and white persons, not merely of the lowest class, but of what are termed the better classes, threw self-restraint aside as quickly and easily as the most uncivilized barbarian, and sailed forth to seek vengeance and to slay.

On a small scale, a similar occurrence took place in Chicago last Thursday, when a miserable negro pickpocket was chased by a howling mob and narrowly escaped death by hanging, at their hands. The idea of leaving malefactors to the justice of the courts never seems to strike the unreasoning crowd. They demand immediate vengeance on the spot, and invariably the mob idea of punishment is disproportionate to the crime.

The alarming feature of all this is that there seems to be an epidemic of riot and disorder due to unreasoning race hatred, and this, too, in Northern states, where the negro had reason to expect fair and just treatment. Such frantic outbreaks are a disgrace to the community in which they occur. Those who
william-fiqua-chicago-1900-08-16.A25: With a mob making war on negroes in New York City, another mob trying to lynch a negro in the streets of Chicago, and a lynching party chasing a negro through a Wisconsin swamp, it won't do for the North to talk very loudly about the way the negroes are treated down South. CROWD ATTACKS PRISONER.
POLICEMEN HAVE TROUBLE IN SAVING COLORED MAN FROM MOB'S FURY COLORED MAN FROM MOB'S FURY IN MADISON SQUARE.
The colored man took part in the arrest of a colored man in Madison Square last night. Vigorous swinging of nightsticks by Policeman Eugene O'Sullivan and several other patrolmen saved the colored man from injury. Several of the men went home with headaches, and two or three had considerable scalp wounds.

The concert by the 12th Regiment Band brought several thousand people to the Square. It was one of the largest crowds of the year. Policeman O'Sullivan was at the Twenty-third-st. side, and when a man told him that three colored men, at the Twenty-sixth-st end of the Square, were ogling white women, he and two other policemen went to the place. The colored men saw the policemen approaching and ran. O'Sullivan chased one under the Dewey Arch and into the Square near the fountain. Twice the policeman slipped and fell, tearing his uniform. He got his man near the fountain. Several hundred very much excited men, who had joined in the pursuit, surrounded the policeman and his prisoner, and some cried "Lynch him!"

The colored man was terrified. He clung to O'Sullivan and begged for protection. The policeman swung his night stick, and knocked several men down. The crowd gave way, but several men managed to land on the colored man's face, and blood flowed from several cuts which they inflicted. Policemen reinforced O'Sullivan, and the prisoner was taken to the station. Several hundred men followed the policemen and their prisoner up Broadway, some shouting from time to time: "Lynch him!"

The colored man described himself as William Jackson, twenty years old, a porter, of No. 225 West Eighteenth-st. He was locked up as a disorderly person.

The crowd did not know why the colored man had been chased, but somebody started the story that he had assaulted a white child. This accounted for the mob's fury.
william-jackson-new-york-1900-08-09.A2:
MOBBED AN INSULTING NEGRO.
Crowd at Madison Square Band Concert Kicks and Cuffs Him Soundly.
While the Twelfth Regiment band was entertaining thousands of persons in Madison Square Park last night three negroes on the Fifth avenue side of the square began to insult women in the crowd and to seize their arms. Some one reported their behavior to Policeman O'Sullivan and he walked up the avenue until he came to the negroes, who immediately ran in different directions. The policeman chased one of them under the Dewey Arch up Broadway and then through Twenty-sixth street into the crowd on the north side of the park. The negro dodged in and out among the crowd and jumped over several benches.

Some one yelled "lynch him: he insulted a girl," and then the crowd went to the assistance of the policeman and the game of tag was promptly ended. The policeman had hard work to get his prisoner to the West Thirtieth street station with a whole skin. As it was, the negro was kicked and rapped a dozen times before he was dragged away from the crowd and 500 persons left the band concert to follow him to the police station.

The prisoner, who said he was William Jackson of 225 West Eighteenth street, was locked up on a charge of disorderly conduct.

FROM GOTHAM

Democratic Opposition to Tammany
Hall Organized.

Ruffian Tore a Diamond Valued at
$700 From a Lady's Ear—Negro
Threatened With Lynching in

BOLD ROBBERY ON A STREET CAR
NEW YORK, August 10.—Democratic opposition to Tammany Hall will be organized in this city regardless of any action that may be taken at the coming State Convention. Mr. Croker is to be sought at home, and an effort will be made to wrest from him control of the municipal patronage.

This matter was discussed yesterday for a full hour by Controner Bird S. Coler and former Senator David Bennett Hill, who met for the purpose in one of the pariors of the Hoffman House. It is not true that Senator Hill has decided to make no contest for supremacy at the State Convention. His attitude there will depend upon the developments of the immediate future.

Should Kings county elect delegates favorable to the candidacy of Controller Coler for Governor, Senator Hill promises to control enough votes from up the State to complete a majority. If this deal is brought about it will mean an alliance of the delegates from Erie and Rensselaer counties with the Tammany forces, as against the remainder of the State. A battle royal will result.

In case Mr. Croker retains control in Kings county all attempt to nominate Mr. Coler will be abandoned, and Senator Hill will then accept the role of leader of the minority in the Convention. He will be ready to put his enemies on the defensive whenever possible, and his one object will be to keep the Tammany organization constantly under observation.

After they separated each declined to be interviewed concerning the subjects discussed by them.

REPUBLICANS UNEASY.

That the members of the Republican National Committee are not entirely pleased with the outlook is proved by the promises which they are practically making to the farmers of the country. From the national headquarters has been issued a proposition for legislation which will most vitally concern the agricultural interests. While the committee does not directly indorse the proposed legislation, it does so indirectly when it includes it in the campaign literature.

John C. Hanley, of St. Paul, Minn., president of the National Cotton Growers' Association and secretary of the National Grain Growers' Association, was at headquarters yesterday in consultation with Joseph H. Manley and Senator Scott. Mr. Hanley had little difficulty in convincing the Republican leaders that the demands of the farmers should be carefully considered.

Pursued by three thousand men and women, William Jackson, colored, darted among the benches in Madison Square Park and through neighboring streets at 10 o'clock last night, trying to avoid capture by Policeman O'Sullivan, of the Criminal Court Squad. He had been accused of insulting women who were enjoying the band concert, and his conduct was reported to the policeman.

THREATENED LYNCHING.

O'Sullivan started after him, but Jackson fled toward the Dewey arch. There was an immense crowd in the park listening to the music. By the time the policeman had elbowed his way through the throng Jackson was half a block away. This did not discourage O'Sullivan, who has a record of 10 2-5s. for sprinting one hundred yards, and he continued to close.

After an exciting chase that effectually broke up the band concert the negro was captured.

Then a new danger threatened Jackson that even the policemen had not counted upon. Some men in the crowd evidently thought that the man had committed a serious offence, and the cry of "Lynch him!" was raised.

Instantly the cry was taken up, and the crowd of angry men swarmed about the trembling prisoner in a threatening manner.

But several other policemen had reinforced O'Sullivan, and they drew their night sticks and formed a circle about the prisoner. They forced a passage through the excited throng and started with Jackson to the West Thirtieth Street police station. There were muttered threats of violence on the way to the station, but no attempt to harm Jackson was made.

BOLD ROBBERY.

One of the boldest robberies reported to the police of this city in several months engaged the attention of Central Office detectives last night.

Mrs. Bessie Krulewitch, the wife of a well to do real estate dealer, living at No. 1632 Madison avenue, while riding westward in a Canal Street surface car at 4 o'clock yesterday afternoon had a diamond earring, valued at $700, torn from her ear by a ruffian, who then sprang from the car to the street and mixed in with the crowd of pedestrians along the sidewalk. There was a detective on the car, but in spite of his presence the thief succeeded in escaping. Detectives were scouring the city last night looking for him, and it was hoped that he would be caught.
